clue.text: Being mad's good for new tricks

indicators.note: good for new says one letter stands in place of another in the word

parts.note: being mad is being manic, wildly excited

explanation.surface: Someone deranged has a knack for learning fresh tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' tells you to put G (good) in place of N (new) in MANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic is conjuring, the art of performing illusions or sleight of hand.

clue.text: Way to survive in Rome?

parts.note: the Latin phrase, as an ancient Roman would put it, for a manner of living; in English it means a working arrangement between parties

explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase literally means a mode of living, used for a practical compromise that lets people coexist.

clue.text: Extremely good place of learning in a Dutch town

indicators.note: in places the university abbreviation within the outer letters
extremely asks for the extreme letters of the word good, its first and last

parts.note: OU is the Open University, a British distance-learning university

explanation.surface: A top-notch college sits in a town in the Netherlands.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university, a standard crossword 'place of learning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gouda is a town in South Holland, famous for the cheese named after it.

clue.text: Time to replace centre of Spanish area with 13 state

indicators.note: says the middle letter of the region's name is swapped out for the time abbreviation

parts.note: Catalonia is a region of north-east Spain around Barcelona

explanation.surface: An instruction for a geography edit: change the heart of a Spanish region.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of CATALONIA (ninth-letter word, fifth letter) is L; 'to replace centre of' puts T there. 13 is STUPOROUS, the answer at 13-down.
explanation.definitionFit: Catatonia is a condition of immobility and unresponsiveness, a stuporous state.

clue.text: Undesirable sorts repeated phrase by artist very loudly

parts.note: a riff is a short musical phrase repeated over and over
RA is a Royal Academician, a crossword artist
FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A musician's repeated motif played very loudly attracts the wrong crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Riff-raff is a disparaging term for disreputable or low-class people.

clue.text: Gone off what top detective did

parts.note: a top detective ran the department, past tense of run
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch, which the top detective ran

explanation.surface: A question about what a senior detective once managed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'what top detective did' as 'ran CID': the head detective ran the Criminal Investigation Department.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has gone off has spoiled, and rancid describes it smelling or tasting stale.

clue.text: Forces clothing on bores

definitions.meaning: the plain working dress worn by soldiers, sailors and airmen
wearies or tires someone out, a verb

explanation.definitionFit: Fatigues are military work clothes, and to fatigue someone is to tire or weary them.

clue.text: Place for a roller to crash?

definitions.text: Place for a roller to crash?

parts.words: Place for a roller to crash?
parts.note: a roller is a kind of pigeon that tumbles in flight, and to crash is slang for going to sleep: where such a bird settles for the night

explanation.definitionFit: A roost is a perch where birds settle to rest or sleep.

clue.text: Blow me —- it's a bean!

definitions.meaning: something you blow into: a small wind instrument, a kind of whistle
a small pale green variety of haricot bean

explanation.definitionFit: A flageolet is both a small fipple flute and a type of young kidney bean.

clue.text: Not sure Welsh poet needed proof of life after death

definitions.text: needed proof of life after death
definitions.note: a verb phrase describing the apostle, standing for the noun naming him

parts.note: not sure means doubting, uncertain
Dylan Thomas, the Welsh poet of Under Milk Wood

explanation.surface: An unsure Welsh writer wanted evidence of an afterlife.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostle Thomas refused to believe in the risen Jesus until he had seen and touched the wounds.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle who demanded evidence of the resurrection gave his name to any habitual sceptic.

clue.text: Pretty morsel cooked for bird

indicators.note: cooked means altered or doctored, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dainty titbit is prepared as a dish of fowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges the twelve letters of 'Pretty morsel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The stormy petrel is a small seabird, once thought to herald bad weather.

clue.text: Timber support around tip

indicators.note: around says the sling is wrapped about the tilting word

parts.note: a sling supports an injured arm
to cant is to tip or tilt

explanation.surface: A wooden brace placed around the end of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Timber' and 'support' look like the definition; 'Timber' alone is it, and 'support' is the sling.
explanation.definitionFit: A scantling is a small beam of timber, or timber cut to set dimensions.

clue.text: Crime financiers turn to?

parts.note: the definite article in the name of the paper financiers read
FT is the Financial Times, the pink British business newspaper

explanation.surface: A suggestion that money men drift into wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests financiers resort to crime; the cryptic reading is that they turn to the FT, the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft is the crime of stealing another person's property.

clue.text: English dogs appeal in pub when out to lunch

indicators.note: dogs means follows closely, so the English abbreviation comes after
in places the appeal inside the pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub
SA, sex appeal, is crossword shorthand for appeal

explanation.surface: An Englishman's dogs bring charm to the pub while he is out at lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dogs' is a verb here, meaning follows closely, not a noun for animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Out to lunch is an idiom for crazy or not all there, as is insane.

clue.text: Son up to no good, shortly to wake up very drunk

indicators.note: no good means wrong or faulty, so the letters of up to are put in a fresh order
shortly says the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to rouse is to wake up

explanation.surface: A boy getting into mischief is soon roused, completely sozzled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to no good' rearranges UPTO into TUPO; 'shortly' cuts the last letter from ROUSE to leave ROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuporous means in a stupor, dazed and insensible, as from heavy drinking.

clue.text: Might he form band with the Stones?

definitions.text: Might he form band with the Stones?

parts.words: Might he form band with the Stones?
parts.note: the surface suggests joining the Rolling Stones; read band as a ring and stones as gems, a craftsman setting them

explanation.definitionFit: A jeweller makes rings and other pieces by setting precious stones in metal.

clue.text: She's featured in Beatles hit, but not the last broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order
says the final letter of the word hit is dropped

explanation.surface: A girl's name appears in a Beatles chart song, though not on the final airing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not the last' drops the T of 'hit' to leave HI; 'broadcast' rearranges BEATLESHI.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a pronoun standing for a woman, and this is a woman's given name.

clue.text: Second try to secure working launch

indicators.note: to secure means to hold fast, so the first pieces close around the working word

parts.note: MO, a moment, is a second
a shot is an attempt or try
on means working, operating

explanation.surface: Another attempt to get a rocket working and off the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an ordinal adjective for 'try'; it is the noun, a brief moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonshot is the launch of a spacecraft to the Moon.

clue.text: Ape's a puppet, we heard subsequently

parts.note: Emu was the arm-puppet of the British entertainer Rod Hull

indicators.note: says the next word is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: subsequently means later

explanation.surface: A monkey turns out to be a puppet, so people say afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Emu was Rod Hull's famously aggressive bird puppet on British TV. 'we heard' turns LATER into its sound-alike LATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape is to imitate, and an emulator is one who imitates or rivals another.

clue.text: After success, go cold

indicators.note: after says the attempt word follows the success word

parts.note: a win is a success
a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: After winning, someone turns frosty.
explanation.definitionFit: Wintry means characteristic of winter, hence cold.

clue.text: Had an evening out with man at club

parts.note: an iron is a golf club
Ed is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man enjoyed a night out at his club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evening out' looks like a night on the town; it means making something even, smoothing creases flat.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron clothes is to even out their creases, so pressing them is an evening out.

clue.text: Fall carrying old flag

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so the fall word encloses the old abbreviation

parts.note: to drop is to fall

explanation.surface: A tumble while bearing an ancient banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts O inside DROP. 'flag' is the verb, to weaken, not a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire or sag, which is to droop.

clue.text: Chaplain departs to shave outside

indicators.note: outside says the shaving word goes around the departs abbreviation

parts.note: to pare is to shave or trim
D is the timetable abbreviation for departs

explanation.surface: A clergyman heads off to have a shave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts PARE around D.
explanation.definitionFit: A padre is a chaplain, especially in the armed forces.

clue.text: A bishop is involved in local story

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up inside, so the bishop piece goes within the local word

parts.note: a native is a local, someone born in the place
RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman figures in a tale told around the parish.
explanation.walkthrough: RR, Right Reverend, is the formal style of an Anglican bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is an account of events, a story.

clue.text: Oddly insolvent, having a small piece of land

indicators.note: oddly asks for the odd-numbered letters of the word insolvent

explanation.surface: Strangely bankrupt, yet owning a little plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' takes the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters of 'insolvent'.
explanation.definitionFit: An islet is a small island, a little patch of land in water.

clue.text: Speaker does his job in another place

definitions.text: Speaker does his job in another place

parts.words: Speaker does his job in another place
parts.note: in the Commons the House of Lords is called another place; the officer who presided over the Lords was its speaker, not the Commons Speaker

explanation.walkthrough: MPs refer to the House of Lords as 'another place'. The surface suggests the Commons Speaker working elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Chancellor traditionally presided over the House of Lords as its speaker.

clue.text: Second East End redevelopment is agreed

indicators.note: redevelopment means rebuilding, so the letters are reconstructed in a new order

explanation.surface: A second wave of rebuilding in London's East End is approved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redevelopment' rearranges S plus EASTEND. The East End is a district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: Assented means gave agreement or consent.

clue.text: Fawlty Towers is very popular with the Spanish

parts.note: hot means very popular, in demand
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A British sitcom is a big hit in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Fawlty Towers was a BBC sitcom set in a chaotic Torquay guest house run by Basil Fawlty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fawlty Towers is the fictional seaside establishment of the sitcom, an example of the answer.
